note: Occupied areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps (chiefly the US Military Academy atlas) and the cited articles; the war had no continuous front lines, so areas show the ground each side held around the places fought over, not exact boundaries.

chapters.title: Lexington, Concord and the siege of Boston
arrows: British march to Concord and back
Bunker Hill: British assault on the Charlestown peninsula
chapters.text: On 19 April 1775 British troops marched from Boston to seize militia weapons at Concord; after shots at Lexington and Concord they were harried all the way back by thousands of militiamen. The militia then besieged British-held Boston. On 17 June the British took the Charlestown peninsula at Bunker Hill, at heavy cost. In March 1776 Washington placed cannon on Dorchester Heights, overlooking the town, and on 17 March the British sailed away.

chapters.title: The fall of New York
arrows: Howe's flank march on Long Island
Howe's landing at Pell's Point and march to White Plains
Cornwallis crosses the Hudson to Fort Lee
chapters.text: General William Howe brought a huge army and fleet to New York, landing on Staten Island on 3 July 1776. On 27 August he outflanked Washington on Long Island, and the Americans slipped across to Manhattan by night. The British landed at Kip's Bay on 15 September and took the city, fought Washington at White Plains on 28 October, and captured Fort Washington, with nearly 3,000 prisoners, on 16 November and Fort Lee four days later. New York stayed in British hands for the rest of the war.

chapters.title: Trenton and Princeton
arrows: Cornwallis pursues Washington across New Jersey
Washington crosses the Delaware to Trenton
chapters.text: Cornwallis chased Washington's shrinking army across New Jersey, and in early December the Americans crossed the Delaware into Pennsylvania while the British spread a chain of posts across the state. On the night of 25 December Washington recrossed the river and surprised the Hessian garrison of Trenton. A week later he slipped round Cornwallis's army and beat the British at Princeton on 3 January 1777, and the British pulled back to New Brunswick, keeping only a few posts in New Jersey.

chapters.title: Saratoga, 1777
arrows: Burgoyne's advance from Canada to Fort Edward
Burgoyne crosses the Hudson to Freeman's Farm
Gates's army moves up to Bemis Heights
chapters.text: In June 1777 General John Burgoyne led an army south from Canada along Lake Champlain to reach Albany. He took Fort Ticonderoga on 6 July and reached Fort Edward on the Hudson on 29 July, but lost a detachment at Bennington on 16 August. Crossing the Hudson, he fought Horatio Gates's growing army at Freeman's Farm on 19 September and at Bemis Heights on 7 October, then fell back to Saratoga, where he surrendered his whole army on 17 October. The victory helped bring France into the war.

chapters.title: Philadelphia and Valley Forge
arrows: Washington's attack at Germantown, and withdrawal
Washington goes into winter quarters at Valley Forge
Clinton marches across New Jersey to Sandy Hook
chapters.text: Howe sailed his army round to the head of Chesapeake Bay, beat Washington at Brandywine on 11 September 1777 and marched into Philadelphia, the American capital, on 26 September. Washington's attack at Germantown on 4 October failed, the British took the Delaware forts in November, and the Continental Army spent a hard winter at Valley Forge. With France now in the war, the British left Philadelphia on 18 June 1778; Washington caught them at Monmouth on 28 June, but they reached New York.

chapters.title: The war turns south: Savannah and Charleston
chapters.text: Hoping for Loyalist support in the South, Britain sent an expedition that captured Savannah on 29 December 1778 and occupied Augusta for a few weeks. A French and American attempt to retake Savannah failed with heavy losses in October 1779. In 1780 Henry Clinton brought a large army from New York and besieged Charleston, which surrendered on 12 May with more than 5,000 American troops, Britain's greatest victory of the war.

chapters.title: Camden to Eutaw Springs
arrows: The Overmountain Men march to Kings Mountain
chapters.text: After Charleston the British set up posts across South Carolina and Georgia, and Cornwallis routed Gates at Camden on 16 August 1780. But backcountry militia destroyed a Loyalist force at Kings Mountain on 7 October and Daniel Morgan beat Tarleton at Cowpens on 17 January 1781. Cornwallis chased Nathanael Greene into North Carolina and won a costly victory at Guilford Court House on 15 March, then marched off to the coast; Greene returned to South Carolina, and by September the British had given up Camden and Ninety Six and held little beyond Charleston and Savannah.

chapters.title: Yorktown, 1781
arrows: Washington and Rochambeau march to Virginia
De Grasse's fleet enters the Chesapeake
chapters.text: Cornwallis took his army into Virginia and in August 1781 fortified Yorktown as a base for the navy. Washington and the French general Rochambeau marched their armies south from New York, while a French fleet under de Grasse sealed Chesapeake Bay and drove off a British fleet on 5 September. Trapped by land and sea and pounded by siege guns, Cornwallis surrendered his army of more than 7,000 on 19 October.

chapters.title: The British leave the South; peace
chapters.text: Yorktown broke Britain's will to continue the war in America: in March 1782 Parliament voted to end offensive operations and Lord North's government fell. British troops left Savannah on 11 July 1782 and Charleston on 14 December 1782, while peace terms were agreed in Paris. The Treaty of Paris, signed on 3 September 1783, recognised the independence of the United States.
